A bullet $B$ is fired from a cannon $C$ at an angle of ${60}^{∘}$ from the horizontal. Given that the bullet's horizontal speed is $300\,\text{ft}/\text{s},$ calculate the actual speed of the bullet in the direction it is traveling.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/fea05a36487813579d4633d9134bdd1d8c4d4bef4e9f57ba997b7b8715d46f32.png)

Let $x$ denote the horizontal distance from the bullet's projection to the cannon, and $z$ be the distance between the bullet and the cannon, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ z & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2x) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =2\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=300\text{ft}/\text{s}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=2\cdot 300=600.
$$

Therefore, the speed of the plane is $600\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.$
